qs.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with urethritis. Cultures are negative for Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Which organism is most likely responsible for this nongonococcal urethritis?
qs.e: Chlamydia trachomatis accounts for 25–60% of nongonococcal urethritis in men and is a leading cause in women. Other bacteria listed are less common primary causes of this specific presentation.
qs.s: Bladder Cancer & Urothelial Neoplasms: Types, Risks, Pathogenesis: MCQs

qs.q: Which surface structure of Neisseria gonorrhoeae undergoes extensive antigenic variation, allowing the bacterium to evade the host immune response and reinfect hosts?
qs.e: Pili (fimbriae) on Neisseria gonorrhoeae undergo high rates of antigenic and phase variation, preventing effective long-term humoral immunity. Ribosomal proteins and core polysaccharides do not undergo rapid surface variation.

qs.q: Ascending infection of the fallopian tubes, known as salpingitis, is commonly caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae and can lead to which major long-term reproductive complication?
qs.e: Chronic inflammation and scarring from gonococcal salpingitis can cause tubal occlusion, resulting in sterility or ectopic pregnancy. The other conditions are not direct sequelae of this ascending bacterial infection.

qs.q: Beta-lactamase production by strains of Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, and Neisseria gonorrhoeae confers resistance against penicillin G. Which one of the following antibiotics is most likely to be effective against all strains of each of the above organisms?
qs.e: Ceftriaxone is a 3rd generation cephalosporin that is β-lactamase stable and has excellent activity against H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis, and N. gonorrhoeae, including β-lactamase-producing strains that are resistant to penicillin G and ampicillin.

qs.q: Ophthalmia neonatorum, a severe conjunctivitis, is associated with Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis, which are sexually transmitted infections.
o: Treponema pallidum and Herpes simplex virus
Human immunodeficiency virus and Hepatitis B virus
qs.e: Ophthalmia neonatorum is a serious eye infection in newborns. The most common causes are Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis, both of which are sexually transmitted infections acquired during passage through the birth canal.

qs.q: Salpingitis, inflammation of the fallopian tubes, is most commonly caused by sexually transmitted infections like Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Syphilis is not a primary cause of salpingitis and does not typically lead to gumma formation in the fallopian tubes.
o: Gonorrhea and Chlamydia; pelvic inflammatory disease
qs.e: Salpingitis is a key component of Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID). The most common causative agents of PID and salpingitis are Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Syphilis does not typically cause salpingitis or gumma formation in the fallopian tubes.

qs.q: A 19-year-old man has urethral discharge. Culture shows Neisseria gonorrhoeae that is β-lactamase positive and highly resistant to tetracycline. Which statement is correct?
o: Treatment with penicillin G is recommended.
Tetracycline would be an effective treatment option.
The resistance to β-lactams indicates a lack of virulence factors.
Ceftriaxone is the recommended first-line treatment.
qs.e: Due to widespread resistance of Neisseria gonorrhoeae to many antibiotics, including β-lactams and tetracyclines, current guidelines recommend ceftriaxone as the first-line treatment. The information provided about β-lactamase positivity and tetracycline resistance highlights the need for appropriate antibiotic choices.

ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a gram‑negative diplococcus causing gonorrhoea, a sexually transmitted infection that can affect the genitourinary tract, rectum, pharynx and eyes. It spreads rapidly, often co‑infects with Chlamydia, and shows increasing antimicrobial resistance.

sections.p: Gonorrhoea is a common STI worldwide, transmitted by sexual contact or perinatally. It can be asymptomatic, especially in women, but may progress to pelvic inflammatory disease, epididymitis, disseminated infection, or neonatal conjunctivitis.
b: Incidence highest in adolescents and young adults
Risk rises with multiple partners, inconsistent condom use, and co‑existing STIs

sections.p: A fastidious, oxidase‑positive, gram‑negative diplococcus that grows on chocolate or Thayer‑Martin agar. It expresses pili for attachment, Opa proteins for invasion, and a variable outer‑membrane protein that evades immunity.
b: Often β‑lactamase positive, high tetracycline resistance

sections.p: Direct mucosal contact transmits the bacteria. After attachment to epithelial cells, it multiplies intracellularly, causing local inflammation and shedding of infected cells that spread to new hosts.
b: Can infect urethra, cervix, rectum, pharynx, conjunctiva

sections.p: Clinical presentations vary by site. Urethritis in men causes purulent discharge and dysuria; cervicitis in women often silent but may cause mucopurulent discharge. Complications include PID, epididymitis, disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI), and neonatal conjunctivitis.
b: PID: lower abdominal pain, cervical motion tenderness, fever
DGI: migratory arthritis, tenosynovitis, pustular rash
Neonatal conjunctivitis: purulent eye discharge within 2‑5 days of birth

sections.p: Combine clinical suspicion with laboratory confirmation. NAAT (nucleic acid amplification test) from site‑specific swabs is the preferred method; Gram stain is useful in symptomatic men.

t.a: NAAT from urethral, cervical, rectal or pharyngeal swab
t.b: Detects bacterial DNA/RNA; a positive result confirms infection even if asymptomatic
Shows intracellular gram‑negative diplococci; positive in men, less sensitive in women
Allows antimicrobial susceptibility testing; essential when resistance is suspected or NAAT unavailable

sections.p: Treat the infection promptly with a dual‑therapy regimen to cover possible co‑infection with Chlamydia and to reduce resistance pressure. Counsel on partner notification and safe sex.
b: Avoid fluoroquinolones and macrolides in many regions due to high resistance
If ceftriaxone unavailable, use spectinomycin where susceptibility confirmed

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams and clinical practice.
b: Gram‑negative intracellular diplococci on urethral smear = gonorrhoea in men
NAAT is the gold standard for all sites; culture needed for susceptibility
Always treat for Chlamydia when gonorrhoea is diagnosed

whenToSeekHelp: Severe pelvic pain with fever (possible PID)
High‑grade fever, joint swelling, or skin pustules (disseminated infection)
Newborn with purulent eye discharge (neonatal conjunctivitis)

faq.q: Why is NAAT preferred over culture?
faq.a: NAAT is more sensitive, works on non‑viable specimens, and provides rapid results, essential for timely treatment.

faq.q: Can gonorrhoea be cured without treating Chlamydia?
faq.a: No; co‑infection is common, and untreated Chlamydia can cause PID and infertility.

faq.q: What if the patient is allergic to ceftriaxone?
faq.a: Use spectinomycin if susceptibility is known, or consult local guidelines for alternative cephalosporins or aztreonam.
